title: A Cognitive Model of the Antecedents and Consequences of Satisfaction Decisions
author_source: Richard L. Oliver, Journal of Marketing Research 17(4), 460-469, 1980, article
note: The founding statement of the expectation-disconfirmation paradigm: satisfaction is modelled as a function of prior expectations plus (dis)confirmation, and satisfaction in turn shifts post-use attitude and purchase intention. Two-stage field study with users and non-users of a flu inoculation, so students can see the pre/post measurement design that every later CS model inherits. Short (10 pages); the path diagram is the one to put on a slide. Caveat: the data context (vaccination) is far from typical marketing cases; pair with a commercial example.
course_use: Core reading for the session on the concept of satisfaction; draw the expectations -> disconfirmation -> satisfaction -> intention chain in class. Access: paid (SAGE), WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: An Investigation into the Determinants of Customer Satisfaction
author_source: Gilbert A. Churchill Jr. and Carol Surprenant, Journal of Marketing Research 19(4), 491-504, 1982, article
note: Classic 3 x 3 factorial experiment (expectation level x performance level) for a nondurable (plant) and a durable (video disc player). For the nondurable the full disconfirmation model holds; for the durable, satisfaction is driven by performance alone and disconfirmation has no effect. This is the best teaching evidence that performance-only measures (later SERVPERF, ACSI 'perceived quality') can be enough. The comparison table of the two product models works well as a discussion slide.
course_use: Core or background reading next to Oliver (1980); use for a debate 'Do we need to measure expectations at all?'. Access: paid (SAGE), WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Defining Consumer Satisfaction
author_source: Joan L. Giese and Joseph A. Cote, Academy of Marketing Science Review 2000(1), 2000, article (online journal)
note: Systematic review of 20 years of satisfaction definitions plus consumer focus groups; concludes that satisfaction is (1) an affective response of varying intensity, (2) focused on a specific object (product, purchase, consumption), (3) occurring at a particular time. Their definitional framework (response / focus / timing) is the cleanest way to show students why survey items must name the object and the time point (transaction-specific vs cumulative). Note: AMS Review was an online journal without DOIs; author-hosted copies circulate but were not verified.
course_use: Background reading for defining the construct; good basis for a seminar exercise where students critique real CSAT survey items against the three components. Access: via ProQuest (login), WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Rediscovering Satisfaction
author_source: Susan Fournier and David Glen Mick, Journal of Marketing 63(4), 5-23, 1999, article
note: Longitudinal, phenomenological (interview-based) study of households adopting technology products. Shows that the comparison-standard (disconfirmation) model fits some consumers but is irrelevant for others; satisfaction emerges as a dynamic, social, emotional process (e.g., 'satisfaction-as-resignation', 'satisfaction-as-delight'). Useful counterweight to purely survey-based CS measurement and to explain why single-item CSAT scores lose meaning.
course_use: Discussion reading in the concept session; contrast with Oliver (1980) and ask what a survey would miss. Access: paid (SAGE), WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Kundenzufriedenheit
author_source: Bernd Stauss, Marketing ZFP 21(1), 5-24, 1999, article (German)
note: German-language overview article on the concept and measurement of customer satisfaction by one of the leading German services-marketing scholars (Eichstätt-Ingolstadt). Discusses the C/D paradigm and approaches to measuring satisfaction in German terminology (Kundenzufriedenheit, Zufriedenheitsmessung); Stauss is known for the distinction between attribute-based and event-based (incident) measurement, but the full text was not checked for this row. One of the few peer-reviewed German sources for this block.
course_use: Background reading in German for students who prefer German literature or write theses in German. Access: paid (Marketing ZFP / Beck eLibrary), WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Customer Satisfaction: A Meta-Analysis of the Empirical Evidence
author_source: David M. Szymanski and David H. Henard, Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science 29(1), 16-35, 2001, article
note: Meta-analysis of the satisfaction literature: equity and disconfirmation have the strongest average correlations with satisfaction; expectations and performance matter less consistently, and measurement/method choices (e.g., scale type, single vs multi-item measures) moderate effect sizes. The summary table of average correlations per antecedent is ideal for a slide ranking the drivers of satisfaction.
course_use: Core reading for 'antecedents of satisfaction'; use the correlation table to test students' intuitions before revealing results. Access: paid (Springer), WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Expectancy-disconfirmation and consumer satisfaction: A meta-analysis
author_source: Tom Schiebler, Nick Lee and Felix C. Brodbeck, Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science 54(1), 91-112, 2026 (online first January 2025), article
note: Up-to-date meta-analytic path analysis of 150 records (N = 58,597): expectations correlate positively with satisfaction (r = .29), there is no evidence for contrast effects, and disconfirmation is a strong mediator. Effects are stronger for predictive (vs normative) expectations, for services, and in cross-sectional designs; an unusual downward publication bias is reported. Shows students that the 40-year-old paradigm still holds and how design choices shape findings.
course_use: Core reading to update Oliver (1980); good for a methods discussion on cross-sectional vs experimental evidence. Access: open access (Springer, CC BY).

title: Customer satisfaction: A multi-level framework
author_source: Vikas Mittal, Sonam Singh and Ashwin Malshe, Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science, online first, 2026, article
note: Very recent synthesis: defines CSAT as a post-consumption judgment of whether customers receive the promised value and separates it from service quality, experience, engagement, loyalty and value. Shows strong convergent validity of commonly used CSAT scales and uses more than 285 million ratings across 1,126 brands to link CSAT with mindset metrics, accounting and stock-market outcomes. Bridges both course emphases (measurement and outcomes) in one paper.
course_use: Core or capstone reading; use its construct-distinction section for the definitions lecture and its outcome evidence as a bridge to the outcomes session. Access: open access (Springer).

title: A framework for comparing customer satisfaction across individuals and product categories
author_source: Michael D. Johnson and Claes Fornell, Journal of Economic Psychology 12(2), 267-286, 1991, article
note: Conceptual foundation of cumulative satisfaction: satisfaction as an overall evaluation built up over the total consumption experience, which makes it comparable across people, firms and categories. This is the theoretical basis for national barometers (Sweden, ACSI, ECSI) and the reason they use cumulative rather than transaction-specific items. A repository copy is openly available in the University of Michigan Deep Blue repository.
course_use: Background reading for the cumulative vs transaction-specific distinction; assign before the ACSI/ECSI session. Access: paid (Elsevier) but open repository copy via Deep Blue (hdl.handle.net/2027.42/29302).

title: Rational and Adaptive Performance Expectations in a Customer Satisfaction Framework
author_source: Michael D. Johnson, Eugene W. Anderson and Claes Fornell, Journal of Consumer Research 21(4), 695-707, 1995, article
note: Market-level model using Swedish Customer Satisfaction Barometer data: satisfaction is treated as a cumulative construct carried over from period to period, while market expectations are largely rational but adapt to recent performance. Useful to show what 'cumulative satisfaction' means empirically (lagged satisfaction as a predictor) and why expectations in index models differ from Oliver's individual-level expectations.
course_use: Advanced background reading (Master level) on cumulative satisfaction. Access: paid (Oxford/JCR), WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: The Antecedents and Consequences of Customer Satisfaction for Firms
author_source: Eugene W. Anderson and Mary W. Sullivan, Marketing Science 12(2), 125-143, 1993, article
note: Field test of the disconfirmation model on 22,300 Swedish customers (1989-1990). Key findings for class: satisfaction is best explained by perceived quality and disconfirmation, expectations have no direct effect, and negative disconfirmation hurts satisfaction and repurchase intention more than positive disconfirmation helps (early evidence of asymmetry). Links concept and outcomes.
course_use: Core reading linking the C/D paradigm to the asymmetry topic; use the asymmetric disconfirmation finding as a lead-in to Kano/three-factor theory. Access: paid (INFORMS), WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: A National Customer Satisfaction Barometer: The Swedish Experience
author_source: Claes Fornell, Journal of Marketing 56(1), 6-21, 1992, article
note: Describes the first national satisfaction index (Swedish Customer Satisfaction Barometer, SCSB, 1989-): cumulative satisfaction measured across 30+ industries and 100+ firms, estimated with a latent-variable (PLS) model. Key teaching points: satisfaction is lower where supply is homogeneous but demand heterogeneous, and higher in industries that depend on repeat business than in captive markets. Introduces the logic of satisfaction as a macro 'quality of output' indicator complementing productivity.
course_use: Core reading for the national-index session; follow with Fornell et al. (1996) on ACSI. Access: paid (SAGE/JSTOR), WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: The American Customer Satisfaction Index: Nature, Purpose, and Findings
author_source: Claes Fornell, Michael D. Johnson, Eugene W. Anderson, Jaesung Cha and Barbara Everitt Bryant, Journal of Marketing 60(4), 7-18, 1996, article
note: The reference description of the ACSI model (expectations, perceived quality, perceived value -> satisfaction -> complaints, loyalty), survey design and PLS estimation. Findings to show students: satisfaction is higher for goods than services and lowest for government agencies; customization matters more than reliability; satisfaction is more quality- than price-driven. The ACSI path model figure is the standard slide for index-based measurement.
course_use: Core reading; reproduce the ACSI path model in class and compare with current scores on theacsi.org. Access: paid (SAGE), WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: The evolution and future of national customer satisfaction index models
author_source: Michael D. Johnson, Anders Gustafsson, Tor Wallin Andreassen, Line Lervik and Jaesung Cha, Journal of Economic Psychology 22(2), 217-245, 2001, article
note: Compares the Swedish, US and emerging European index models and tests modifications with Norwegian Customer Satisfaction Barometer data: replacing expectations with corporate image, splitting loyalty from complaint handling, adding affective and calculative commitment. Good to explain why ECSI/EPSI add 'image' and drop some ACSI paths.
course_use: Background reading for comparing ACSI vs ECSI/EPSI model structures; students can sketch both models side by side. Access: paid (Elsevier), WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Modelling customer satisfaction and loyalty on aggregate levels: Experience from the ECSI pilot study
author_source: Claes Cassel and Jan A. Eklöf, Total Quality Management 12(7-8), 834-841, 2001, article
note: Reports the European Customer Satisfaction Index (ECSI) pilot across 11 countries and industries such as telecoms, banking and supermarkets; shows that one common structural model (image, expectations, perceived product and service quality, value, satisfaction, loyalty) is robust enough for pan-European use, while 'perceived value' is the hardest construct to measure. Origin of today's EPSI Rating (incl. Austria).
course_use: Background reading for the European index model; connect to current EPSI country reports. Access: paid (Taylor & Francis), WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: The Austrian Customer Satisfaction Barometer (ACSB) - A pilot study
author_source: Peter Hackl, Dieter Scharitzer and Reinhard Zuba, der markt 35(2), 86-94, 1996, article
note: Pilot study for an Austrian national satisfaction barometer modelled on the Swedish SCSB and ACSI, by authors from WU Vienna. Describes model, sampling and first results, i.e., a local, WU-specific example of how national CS indices were transferred to Austria. Short article (9 pages) published in the Austrian marketing journal der markt.
course_use: Background reading with local relevance for WU students; use as an anchor for discussing whether Austria has (or needs) a national index today. Access: paid (Springer), WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: A Conceptual Model of Service Quality and Its Implications for Future Research
author_source: A. Parasuraman, Valarie A. Zeithaml and Leonard L. Berry, Journal of Marketing 49(4), 41-50, 1985, article
note: The GAP model of service quality from focus groups in four service businesses: perceived quality = gap 5 between expected and perceived service, caused by four provider gaps (knowledge, standards, delivery, communication), and ten original quality determinants later condensed into the five SERVQUAL dimensions. The gaps diagram is a must-have slide for distinguishing service quality from satisfaction.
course_use: Core reading for the service-quality measurement session; students map a real complaint to gaps 1-4. Access: paid (SAGE), WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Measuring Service Quality: A Reexamination and Extension
author_source: J. Joseph Cronin Jr. and Steven A. Taylor, Journal of Marketing 56(3), 55-68, 1992, article
note: Introduces SERVPERF: the 22 SERVQUAL perception items without expectation scores outperform the perception-minus-expectation gap score in four industries (banking, pest control, dry cleaning, fast food). Also argues that service quality is an antecedent of satisfaction and that satisfaction has the stronger effect on purchase intentions. Read together with the 1994 SERVPERF vs SERVQUAL reply (JM 58(1), 125-131).
course_use: Core reading paired with Parasuraman et al. (1985/1988); debate the gap-score vs performance-only question. Access: paid (SAGE), WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Importance-Performance Analysis
author_source: John A. Martilla and John C. James, Journal of Marketing 41(1), 77-79, 1977, article
note: The original IPA paper (only three pages): attribute importance and performance ratings are plotted in a 2 x 2 grid with four action quadrants ('Concentrate here', 'Keep up the good work', 'Low priority', 'Possible overkill'), illustrated with an automobile dealer's service department. The quadrant chart is the single most important figure for this course block; the paper also already discusses crosshair placement (means vs medians).
course_use: Core reading; reproduce the four-quadrant chart and have students build their own IPA in Excel with a short class survey. Access: paid (SAGE/JSTOR), WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: The Performance-Importance Response Function: Observations and Implications
author_source: Scott E. Sampson and Michael J. Showalter, The Service Industries Journal 19(3), 1-25, 1999, article
note: Shows empirically that attribute importance is not a fixed scalar but a function of performance: as performance on an attribute improves, its stated importance changes, which can reverse IPA improvement priorities. This is the key early critique of IPA's independence assumption and a precursor of the three-factor/Kano-based revisions.
course_use: Background reading for the 'IPA critique' session; ask students what happens to a 'Concentrate here' attribute after it has been fixed. Access: paid (Taylor & Francis), WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Revisiting importance-performance analysis
author_source: Haemoon Oh, Tourism Management 22(6), 617-627, 2001, article
note: Critical review of IPA practice in hospitality and tourism with re-analysis of published data: questions the meaning of 'importance', the independence of importance and performance, the choice of crosshairs (scale mean vs data mean) and the use of an iso-rating (diagonal) line. A compact checklist of everything that can go wrong in an IPA, very useful before a student project.
course_use: Core methods reading before any student IPA project; turn Oh's issues into a grading checklist. Access: paid (Elsevier), WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Importance-performance analysis revisited: the role of the factor structure of customer satisfaction
author_source: Kurt Matzler, Elmar Sauerwein and Kenneth A. Heischmidt, The Service Industries Journal 23(2), 112-129, 2003, article
note: Austrian-led (Innsbruck) study of bank customers showing that traditional IPA can be misleading when attributes are basic, performance or excitement factors, because their importance depends on their performance. Presents an analytical procedure (dummy-variable regression) to identify the factor type and shows how to extend the IPA grid accordingly. A direct bridge between IPA and the Kano/three-factor model.
course_use: Core reading for the IPA session (the 'revisited' paper the course asks for); compare its revised grid with Martilla and James (1977). Access: paid (Taylor & Francis), WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: The asymmetric relationship between attribute-level performance and overall customer satisfaction: a reconsideration of the importance-performance analysis
author_source: Kurt Matzler, Franz Bailom, Hans H. Hinterhuber, Birgit Renzl and Johann Pichler, Industrial Marketing Management 33(4), 271-277, 2004, article
note: B2B study (customers of an automotive supplier) by the Innsbruck group: dummy-variable regression confirms asymmetric effects of attribute performance on overall satisfaction, and the authors show that recommendations from a traditional IPA would be misleading. Short (7 pages) and the most-cited version of the 'IPA must be revised' argument; the side-by-side comparison of IPA quadrant vs factor classification is the slide to show.

title: The factor structure of customer satisfaction: An empirical test of the importance grid and the penalty-reward-contrast analysis
author_source: Kurt Matzler and Elmar Sauerwein, International Journal of Service Industry Management 13(4), 314-332, 2002, article

The two methods do not converge, so the importance grid's validity is questioned. Excellent for teaching that the classification depends on the method chosen.

author_source: Kurt Matzler, Josef A. Mazanec, Andreas Ströbl and Karin Teichmann, Problems and Perspectives in Management 19(2), 398-417, 2021, article

title: Importance-performance analysis (IPA): quadrant grid, crosshair choice and diagonal (iso-rating) line
author_source: Method; key comparison source: Donald R. Bacon, International Journal of Market Research 45(1), 1-15, 2003, article
note: IPA plots mean attribute importance against mean attribute performance in a 2 x 2 grid (Martilla and James 1977). Bacon compares IPA variants across 15 datasets and shows that the traditional quadrant approach can be misleading and that regression-derived (indirect) importance can also mislead; he identifies a diagonal-line (importance-performance gap) approach as most valid and offers a validity check. Teaching steps: choose attributes, measure importance and performance, decide on crosshairs (scale mid-point vs data means), add the iso-rating line, interpret quadrants.

title: Revised IPA with three-factor theory and benchmarking (derived importance, competitor comparison)

title: Penalty-reward contrast analysis (PRCA) and asymmetric impact-performance analysis (AIPA)
author_source: Method; review source: Tahir Albayrak and Meltem Caber, Total Quality Management & Business Excellence 24(11-12), 1288-1300, 2013, article
note: PRCA (Brandt) regresses overall satisfaction on two dummy variables per attribute (low and high performance) to estimate a penalty and a reward; their relative size classifies attributes as basic (dissatisfier), performance (hybrid) or excitement (satisfier). The review shows inconsistent practice in defining low/high cut-offs, standardised vs unstandardised coefficients and classification rules, proposes a standard procedure, and demonstrates that different choices change results on the same data. AIPA plots the impact asymmetry against performance.

The paper also argues that direct and indirect 'importance' measure different constructs, a key conceptual point for IPA users.
course_use: Advanced lab: compute RIOS and IA from PRCA coefficients and compare with the IPA grid. Access: paid (Emerald), WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: SERVQUAL (gap scores) vs SERVPERF (performance only)
author_source: Method; meta-analytic source: François A. Carrillat, Fernando Jaramillo and Jay P. Mulki, International Journal of Service Industry Management 18(5), 472-490, 2007, article

title: How Main Street Drives Wall Street: Customer (Dis)satisfaction, Short Sellers, and Abnormal Returns
author_source: Malshe, A., Colicev, A. & Mittal, V., Journal of Marketing Research 57(6), 1055-1075, 2020, article
note: 273 firms, quarterly data 2007-2017: short interest mediates the effect of satisfaction on abnormal returns. A one-unit increase in satisfaction goes with +0.56 percentage points abnormal return, a one-unit increase in dissatisfaction with -1.34 pp, so dissatisfaction weighs more than twice as much.
course_use: Core recent reading with clean effect sizes and an asymmetry message (links to IPA and asymmetric attribute impact). Open access (hybrid, SAGE).

title: Old signals, new era: Reconsidering how customer satisfaction and employee satisfaction impact shareholder wealth
author_source: Zamudio, C., Mah, S. & Swaminathan, V., Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science 54(1), 113-134, 2026 (online 2025), article
note: Social-media and retail-investor era: unanticipated increases in employee satisfaction reduce shareholder wealth when customer satisfaction has also increased (negative joint effect), more so with high social-media visibility and industry concentration.
course_use: Recent reading for discussing service-profit-chain assumptions; open access (hybrid, Springer).

title: The Customer Knows Best: The Investment Value of Consumer Opinions
author_source: Huang, J., Journal of Financial Economics 128(1), 164-182, 2018, article
note: 14.5 million Amazon reviews 2004-2015: a long-short portfolio on abnormal customer ratings earns about 56-73 basis points per month without reversal; ratings predict revenue and earnings surprises. Online reviews act as a real-time satisfaction signal for investors.
course_use: Finance-journal evidence connecting online reviews (a satisfaction proxy) to stock returns; good for a 'big data satisfaction' session. Free SSRN version (abstract 2758807); journal WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: On the value relevance of customer satisfaction. Multiple drivers and multiple markets
author_source: Raithel, S., Sarstedt, M., Scharf, S. & Schwaiger, M., Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science 40(4), 509-525, 2012, article
note: German authors (LMU Munich); car brands 2004-2008 in the US, UK and Germany: investors react to changes in the perceived product-quality driver of satisfaction but not to cost of ownership or dealer service quality; US information dominates.
course_use: Bridges attribute-level satisfaction measurement (driver/IPA logic) and investor value; DACH relevance. WU-Lizenz prüfen (paid journal)

title: Satisfaction, Complaint, and the Stock Value Gap
author_source: Luo, X. & Homburg, C., Journal of Marketing 72(4), 29-43, 2008, article

course_use: Background on the asymmetry of dissatisfaction for investors. WU-Lizenz prüfen (paid journal)

title: Customer Satisfaction, Analyst Stock Recommendations, and Firm Value
author_source: Luo, X., Homburg, C. & Wieseke, J., Journal of Marketing Research 47(6), 1041-1058, 2010, article
note: Longitudinal ACSI-analyst data: positive changes in satisfaction improve analyst recommendations and reduce their dispersion (more so under high competition and market uncertainty); recommendations partially mediate the effect of satisfaction on abnormal returns and on systematic and idiosyncratic risk.

title: Is customer satisfaction a relevant metric for financial analysts?
author_source: Ngobo, P.-V., Casta, J.-F. & Ramond, O., Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science 40(3), 480-508, 2012, article

title: Does Customer Satisfaction Matter to Investors? Findings from the Bond Market
author_source: Anderson, E.W. & Mansi, S.A., Journal of Marketing Research 46(5), 703-714, 2009, article

author_source: Himme, A. & Fischer, M., International Journal of Research in Marketing 31(2), 224-238, 2014, article

title: Customer satisfaction and the cost of capital
author_source: Truong, C., Nguyen, T.H. & Huynh, T.D., Review of Accounting Studies 26(1), 293-342, 2021, article

author_source: Lim, L.G., Tuli, K.R. & Grewal, R., Journal of Marketing 84(4), 23-44, 2020, article

title: Customer Satisfaction and Firm Profits in Monopolies: A Study of Utilities
author_source: Bhattacharya, A., Morgan, N.A. & Rego, L.L., Journal of Marketing Research 58(1), 202-222, 2021, article

title: Neglected Outcomes of Customer Satisfaction
author_source: Luo, X. & Homburg, C., Journal of Marketing 71(2), 133-149, 2007, article

title: The complex firm financial effects of customer satisfaction improvements
author_source: Guenther, M. & Guenther, P., International Journal of Research in Marketing 38(3), 639-662, 2021, article

author_source: Anderson, E.W., Marketing Letters 7(3), 265-274, 1996, article

title: Do Satisfied Customers Really Pay More? A Study of the Relationship between Customer Satisfaction and Willingness to Pay
author_source: Homburg, C., Koschate, N. & Hoyer, W.D., Journal of Marketing 69(2), 84-96, 2005, article
note: Two experiments (lab study and real usage over time; German lead authors): satisfaction strongly raises willingness to pay along an inverse S-shaped curve (disappointment theory), flat in the middle and steep at the extremes; cumulative satisfaction matters more than transaction-specific satisfaction. course_use: Core reading for the price-premium outcome; show the curve and discuss what it implies for target satisfaction levels. WU-Lizenz prüfen (paid journal)

title: Customer satisfaction: Cost driver or value driver? Empirical evidence from the financial services industry
author_source: Terpstra, M. & Verbeeten, F.H.M., European Management Journal 32(3), 499-508, 2014, article

title: The Impact of Customer Satisfaction on Share-of-Wallet in a Business-to-Business Environment
author_source: Keiningham, T. L., Perkins-Munn, T., Evans, H., Journal of Service Research 6(1), 37-50, 2003, article

author_source: Rego, L.L., Morgan, N.A. & Fornell, C., Journal of Marketing 77(5), 1-20, 2013, article

author_source: Gupta, S. & Zeithaml, V., Marketing Science 25(6), 718-739, 2006, article (review)

author_source: Zeithaml, V.A., Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science 28(1), 67-85, 2000, article (review)

title: Nonlinear and asymmetric returns on customer satisfaction: do they vary across situations and consumers?
author_source: Eisenbeiss, M., Cornelißen, M., Backhaus, K. & Hoyer, W.D., Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science 42(3), 242-263, 2014, article

title: Does customer satisfaction increase firm performance? An application of American Customer Satisfaction Index (ACSI)
author_source: Sun, K.-A. & Kim, D.-Y., International Journal of Hospitality Management 35, 68-77, 2013, article
note: Hotels, restaurants and airlines (ACSI): satisfaction positively affects profit margin, ROA, ROE and market value added. Note: this is an industry panel study, not a meta-analysis.

title: Linking customer satisfaction with financial performance: an empirical study of Scandinavian banks
author_source: Eklof, J., Podkorytova, O. & Malova, A., Total Quality Management & Business Excellence 31(15-16), 1684-1702, 2020, article

title: Der Zusammenhang zwischen Mitarbeiter- und Kundenzufriedenheit: Eine Metaanalyse
author_source: Gerpott, T.J. & Paukert, M., Zeitschrift für Personalforschung / German Journal of Human Resource Management 25(1), 28-54, 2011, article (German)

title: Der Zusammenhang zwischen Mitarbeiter- und Kundenzufriedenheit - Eine dyadische Analyse
author_source: Homburg, C. & Stock, R., Zeitschrift für Betriebswirtschaft 71(7), 789-806, 2001, article (German)
note: German dyadic study (matched employees and customers) showing that employee satisfaction drives customer satisfaction, with moderators such as interaction intensity; part of the Homburg/Stock-Homburg work that treats the positive effect of customer satisfaction on firm success as established.

title: Revisiting the Satisfaction-Loyalty Relationship: Empirical Generalizations and Directions for Future Research
author_source: Kumar, V., Dalla Pozza, I., Ganesh, J., Journal of Retailing 89(3), 246-262, 2013, article (review)
note: Review of satisfaction-loyalty research yielding empirical generalizations: the link is positive but satisfaction alone explains little variance in loyalty (especially behavioural loyalty); models with moderators/mediators predict better; the link can change over time. author_source: Curtis, T., Abratt, R., Rhoades, D., Dion, P., Journal of Consumer Satisfaction, Dissatisfaction and Complaining Behavior 24, 1-26, 2011, article (meta-analysis)

note: Meta-analysis of loyalty predictors: trust has the strongest effect; satisfaction effects are weaker for short purchase cycles and weaker in B2B than B2C; attitudinal loyalty measures are a plausible surrogate for behavioural ones; single-item loyalty measures yield weaker effects. Useful for moderators (purchase cycle, B2B vs B2C).

title: Customer Evaluations of Service Complaint Experiences: Implications for Relationship Marketing
author_source: Tax, S. S., Brown, S. W., Chandrashekaran, M., Journal of Marketing 62(2), 60-76, 1998, article

title: Service Recovery Paradox: A Meta-Analysis
author_source: de Matos, C. A., Henrique, J. L., Rossi, C. A. V., Journal of Service Research 10(1), 60-77, 2007, article (meta-analysis)

title: A Meta-Analysis of Organizational Complaint Handling and Customer Responses
author_source: Gelbrich, K., Roschk, H., Journal of Service Research 14(1), 24-43, 2011, article (meta-analysis)
note: Meta-analytic path model: organisational responses (compensation, employee behaviour, procedures) -> justice -> post-complaint satisfaction -> loyalty and WOM. title: A meta-analysis of satisfaction with complaint handling in services
author_source: Orsingher, C., Valentini, S., de Angelis, M., Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science 38(2), 169-186, 2010, article (meta-analysis)

title: The service recovery paradox: true but overrated?
author_source: Michel, S., Meuter, M. L., International Journal of Service Industry Management 19(4), 441-457, 2008, article

author_source: Homburg, C., Fürst, A., Journal of Marketing 69(3), 95-114, 2005, article

title: Customers' emotions in service failure and recovery: a meta-analysis
author_source: Valentini, S., Orsingher, C., Polyakova, A., Marketing Letters 31, 199-213, 2020, article (meta-analysis)

title: Online service failure and recovery: An integrated meta-analytic perspective of attribution and justice theories
author_source: Das, M., et al., Journal of Business Research, 2026, article (MASEM)
note: 147 studies, 82,901 individuals, 24 countries: online failure causes -> complaints; effective complaint handling -> justice -> positive emotions -> loyalty, trust, WOM and less switching; moderators include brand prestige, offering type, purchase frequency, age, income, country development. Digital-era update.
course_use: Use for digital complaint handling and recovery; recent evidence. Access: WU-Lizenz prüfen (paid journal; access via WU library e-journals).

title: Consumer Complaint Intentions and Behavior: Definitional and Taxonomical Issues
author_source: Singh, J., Journal of Marketing 52(1), 93-107, 1988, article
note: Taxonomy of dissatisfaction responses: voice (to seller), private responses (exit, negative WOM) and third-party responses. Operationalises Hirschman's exit-voice logic for marketing.
course_use: Use to structure the dissatisfaction-outcomes slide (exit, voice, negative WOM, third-party). Access: WU-Lizenz prüfen (paid journal; access via WU library e-journals).

title: Customer Switching Behavior in Service Industries: An Exploratory Study
author_source: Keaveney, S. M., Journal of Marketing 59(2), 71-82, 1995, article

title: The push-pull-mooring model of consumer service switching: a meta-analytical review to guide future research
author_source: Marx, T., Journal of Service Theory and Practice, 2025, article (meta-analysis, MASEM)

course_use: Recent synthesis for dissatisfaction -> switching; good framework slide. Access: WU-Lizenz prüfen (paid journal; access via WU library e-journals).

author_source: Garbarino, E., Johnson, M. S., Journal of Marketing 63(2), 70-87, 1999, article

author_source: Palmatier, R. W., Dant, R. P., Grewal, D., Evans, K. R., Journal of Marketing 70(4), 136-153, 2006, article (meta-analysis)

title: A Meta-Analysis of Satisfaction in Marketing Channel Relationships
author_source: Geyskens, I., Steenkamp, J.-B. E. M., Kumar, N., Journal of Marketing Research 36(2), 223-238, 1999, article (meta-analysis)

title: The link between salespeople's job satisfaction and customer satisfaction in a business-to-business context: A dyadic analysis
author_source: Homburg, C., Stock, R. M., Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science 32(2), 144-158, 2004, article
note: Dyadic B2B data across industries: salespeople's job satisfaction positively affects customer satisfaction via emotional contagion; link stronger with frequent interaction, high customer integration and high product innovativeness. Satisfaction mirror in B2B.

title: A Meta-Analysis of Relationships Linking Employee Satisfaction to Customer Responses
author_source: Brown, S. P., Lam, S. K., Journal of Retailing 84(3), 243-255, 2008, article (meta-analysis)
note: Employee job satisfaction is positively related to customer satisfaction and perceived service quality; perceived service quality fully mediates the employee satisfaction -> customer satisfaction link; moderated by industry and method factors.
course_use: Core meta-analysis for the satisfaction mirror; show the mediation path. Access: WU-Lizenz prüfen (paid journal; access via WU library e-journals).

title: A cross-lagged test of the association between customer satisfaction and employee job satisfaction in a relational context
author_source: Zablah, A. R., Carlson, B. D., Donavan, D. T., Maxham, J. G., III, Brown, T. J., Journal of Applied Psychology 101(5), 743-755, 2016, article

title: The Service-Profit Chain: A Meta-Analytic Test of a Comprehensive Theoretical Framework
author_source: Hogreve, J., Iseke, A., Derfuss, K., Eller, T., Journal of Marketing 81(3), 41-61, 2017, article (meta-analysis)
note: First comprehensive meta-analytic test of the service-profit chain: all links significant but effect sizes vary by service type; internal service quality affects performance through paths beyond employee satisfaction; challenges the rule to always maximise employee satisfaction and external quality.
course_use: Use as the evidence summary for the service-profit chain; German authors. Access: WU-Lizenz prüfen (paid journal; access via WU library e-journals).

title: Social Identity and the Service-Profit Chain
author_source: Homburg, C., Wieseke, J., Hoyer, W. D., Journal of Marketing 73(2), 38-54, 2009, article

title: Customer Engagement Behavior: Theoretical Foundations and Research Directions
author_source: van Doorn, J., Lemon, K. N., Mittal, V., Nass, S., Pick, D., Pirner, P., Verhoef, P. C., Journal of Service Research 13(3), 253-266, 2010, article (conceptual)

author_source: Pansari, A., Kumar, V., Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science 45(3), 294-311, 2017, article (conceptual)

title: Customer engagement in social media: a framework and meta-analysis
author_source: Santini, F. de O., Ladeira, W. J., Pinto, D. C., Herter, M. M., Sampaio, C. H., Babin, B. J., Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science 48(6), 1211-1228, 2020, article (meta-analysis)

author_source: Yi, Y., Gong, T., Journal of Business Research 66(9), 1279-1284, 2013, article

author_source: Lee, Z. W. Y., Chan, T. K. H., Chong, A. Y.-L., Thadani, D. R., Industrial Marketing Management 77, 90-101, 2019, article

title: Satisfaction: A Behavioral Perspective on the Consumer (2nd ed.)
author_source: Richard L. Oliver; M.E. Sharpe 2010, reissued by Routledge 2015 (e-ISBN 9781315700892), approx. 520-540 pp., book

author_source: Christian Homburg (Hrsg.); Springer Gabler, 9th ed. 2016, 591 pp., edited book

author_source: Roland T. Rust, Anthony J. Zahorik, Timothy L. Keiningham; Probus, 1994, book

title: Enterprise Rent-A-Car ESQi: one top-box question, promotions tied to scores

Caveat: the effect sizes come from the article's model (often quoted second-hand), and Sears' later decline is a good discussion point.
